claim: The Hsp70 chaperone system is integrated into a myriad of biochemical processes that are critical for cellular proteostasis.
source: The Hsp70 chaperone system is integrated into a myriad of biochemical processes that are critical for cellular proteostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about Hsp70's role, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Detailed pictures of Hsp70 bound with peptides have emerged.
source: Although detailed pictures of Hsp70 bound with peptides have emerged, correspondingly detailed structural information on complexes with folding-competent substrates remains lacking.
evidence: This statement refers to existing structural studies in the literature.

claim: Detailed structural information on Hsp70 complexes with folding-competent substrates remains lacking.
source: Although detailed pictures of Hsp70 bound with peptides have emerged, correspondingly detailed structural information on complexes with folding-competent substrates remains lacking.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: DnaK binds to as many as four distinct sites on hTRF1.
source: Here we report a methyl-TROSY based solution NMR study showing that the Escherichia coli version of Hsp70, DnaK, binds to as many as four distinct sites on a small 53-residue client protein, hTRF1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by NMR experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A fraction of hTRF1 chains are bound to two DnaK molecules simultaneously.
source: A fraction of hTRF1 chains are also bound to two DnaK molecules simultaneously, resulting in a mixture of DnaK-substrate sub-ensembles that are structurally heterogeneous.
evidence: This finding is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The interactions of Hsp70 with a client protein at different sites results in a fuzzy chaperone-substrate ensemble.
source: The interactions of Hsp70 with a client protein at different sites results in a fuzzy chaperone-substrate ensemble and suggests a mechanism for Hsp70 function whereby the structural heterogeneity of released substrate molecules enables them to circumvent kinetic traps in their conformational free energy landscape and fold efficiently to the native state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple binding sites and conformational heterogeneity.

claim: The Hsp70 chaperone system plays a vital role in quality control by overseeing the integrity of the cellular proteome in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans.
source: The Hsp70 chaperone system plays a vital role in quality control by overseeing the integrity of the cellular proteome in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans (Balchin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hsp70 performs ATP-dependent interactions with client proteins that impart directionality to cellular processes such as protein folding.
source: Hsp70 performs a staggering array of functions and its ATP-dependent interaction with client proteins imparts directionality to a number of cellular processes such as protein folding (Hartl et al., 2011), translocation (Kang et al., 1990; Pilon and Schekman, 1999; Mayer, 2013), disaggregation (Nillegoda et al., 2015; Mogk et al., 2015) and oligomer disassembly (Böcking et al., 2011; De Los Rios and Goloubinoff, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hsp70 is able to interact with clients having a broad range of conformations.
source: Hsp70 is able to interact with clients having a broad range of conformations (Schlecht et al., 2011; Mashaghi et al., 2016), including unfolded polypeptides emerging from the ribosome (Teter et al., 1999; Deuerling et al., 1999; Willmund et al., 2013), native proteins such as the heat shock transcription factor (Rodriguez et al., 2008), macromolecular assemblies including clathrin-coated vesicles (Sousa et al., 2016), as well as non-native misfolded and aggregated polypeptide chains (Szabo et al., 1994; Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Goloubinoff and De Los Rios, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The multitude of client conformations that Hsp70 recognizes is in sharp contrast to the simplicity of its client binding-site architecture.
source: The multitude of client conformations that Hsp70 recognizes and the diversity of functions it carries out are in sharp contrast to the simplicity of its client binding-site architecture (Clerico et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Hsp70 interacts with client substrates through its C-terminal domain, which is composed of a β-sandwich subdomain that includes a substrate binding cleft and an α-helical lid.
source: Hsp70 interacts with client substrates through its C-terminal domain, which is composed of a β-sandwich subdomain that includes a substrate binding cleft and an α-helical lid (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and Figure 1A showing the domain architecture.

claim: Short peptides bind Hsp70 in an extended conformation with only five residues contacting Hsp70.
source: Both crystal- (Zhu et al., 1996; Zahn et al., 2013) and NMR-derived structures (Stevens et al., 2003) show that short peptides bind Hsp70 in an extended conformation with only five residues contacting Hsp70.
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal and NMR structures.

claim: The peptide is stabilized in the binding pocket by hydrogen bonds between its backbone and binding cavity forming loops in Hsp70, as well as by hydrophobic interactions between the peptide core and conserved Ile, Leu and Met residues of the binding cleft.
source: The peptide is stabilized in the binding pocket by hydrogen bonds between its backbone and binding cavity forming loops in Hsp70, as well as by hydrophobic interactions between the peptide core and conserved Ile, Leu and Met residues of the binding cleft (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The binding pocket of Hsp70 may possess considerable intrinsic flexibility.
source: Crystal structures of a number of peptides bound to Hsp70 have been solved with Ile, Leu, Pro and the unnatural amino acid cyclohexylalanine occupying the central position of the binding pocket, suggesting that the pocket may possess considerable intrinsic flexibility (Zahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from crystal structures cited in the literature.

claim: hTRF1 is a 53-residue three-helix bundle belonging to the homeodomain family of proteins.
source: In order to obtain insight into the molecular details of Hsp70-substrate interactions we have used the model substrate hTRF1 (Figure 1C), a 53-residue three-helix bundle belonging to the homeodomain family of proteins (Gianni et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and Figure 1C showing the structure.

claim: hTRF1 is only marginally stable and its native conformation is in equilibrium with an unfolded state that is populated at 4.2% with a lifetime of 2.9 ms at 35°C.
source: hTRF1 is only marginally stable and its native conformation is in equilibrium with an unfolded state that is populated at 4.2% and only transiently formed with a lifetime of 2.9 ms (35°C) (Sekhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: hTRF1 has one predicted strong DnaK binding site centred at Leu 31 and two additional weak sites around residues 16 and 42.
source: This substrate has one predicted (Rüdiger et al., 1997) strong DnaK binding site centred at Leu 31 and two additional weak sites around residues 16 and 42 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a prediction algorithm cited and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DnaK-bound hTRF1 is globally unfolded but retains as much as 40% residual secondary structure in regions distal to the DnaK binding site.
source: We have previously shown that hTRF1 interacts with DnaK at its canonical binding site and while DnaK-bound hTRF1 is globally unfolded, secondary structural propensities are not affected in substrate regions distal to the DnaK binding site, with as much as 40% residual secondary structure retained (Sekhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Transient long-range native and non-native tertiary interactions present in the unfolded state of hTRF1 are disrupted in the DnaK-bound form.
source: In contrast, a series of spin relaxation experiments established that transient long-range native and non-native tertiary interactions that are present in the unfolded state of hTRF1 are disrupted in the bound form (Sekhar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: DnaK maintains hTRF1 in a globally unfolded conformation throughout the entire chaperone nucleotide cycle.
source: Interestingly, despite the fact that DnaK undergoes large conformational changes between ATP and ADP bound states the tethered hTRF1 is maintained in a globally unfolded conformation throughout the entire chaperone nucleotide cycle (Sekhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Residues 27–39 of hTRF1 were invisible in TROSY-based 1H-15N spectra of U-2H/15N hTRF1 bound to U-2H DnaK/ADP.
source: Our initial studies using 1H-15N NMR spectroscopy could not detect hTRF1 residues located at or near the DnaK binding site (residues 27–39 were invisible), because the relevant 1H-15N correlations were not visible in TROSY-based spectra of U-2H/15N hTRF1 bound to U-2H DnaK/ADP that reflects both the slow rotational tumbling of the ~80 kDa DnaK-hTRF1 complex and potentially also conformational heterogeneity at the binding site (see below).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the authors' previous studies.

claim: The methyl-TROSY technique takes advantage of favorable relaxation properties of the 13C and 1H methyl spins during magnetization transfer in a heteronuclear multiple quantum correlation (HMQC) experiment.
source: The methyl-TROSY technique takes advantage of favorable relaxation properties of the 13C and 1H methyl spins during magnetization transfer in a heteronuclear multiple quantum correlation (HMQC) experiment, where one of the two magnetization transfer pathways is effectively immune to intra-methyl dipolar relaxation (Tugarinov et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the methodological basis of methyl-TROSY, supported by a citation.

claim: Upon addition of 2-fold excess U-2H DnaK/ADP, at least five peaks are observed for Ile 29 at chemical shifts distinct from the free state.
source: However, upon addition of 2-fold excess U-2H DnaK/ADP, at least five peaks are observed for Ile 29 at chemical shifts that are distinct from the resonance position of Ile 29 in the free state, labeled as A-E in Figure 2B, suggesting that there are multiple conformations of DnaK-bound hTRF1.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Multiple conformations of DnaK-bound hTRF1 exist as established by diffusion coefficient measurements.
source: In order to ensure that all the new Ile peaks arise from chaperone-bound hTRF1 molecules, we measured peak-specific diffusion coefficients using a 2D 1H-13C HMQC-based pulsed field gradient (PFG) diffusion experiment. Of the diffusion coefficients that could be quantified reliably, those measured from the new peaks are very similar and are smaller than the free hTRF1 diffusion rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), establishing the existence of multiple DnaK-bound states of hTRF1 and thus conformational heterogeneity in the bound ensemble.
evidence: This is supported by diffusion coefficient data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Extra peaks for DnaK corresponding to Ile 401 and Ile 438 were observed upon addition of hTRF1.
source: Upon addition of 2-fold excess U-2H hTRF1 several new peaks appeared in the 1H-13C HMQC spectrum of IM-13CH3 labeled DnaK/ADP (compare Figure 2D and E). These could be assigned via a methyl-NOESY data set recorded on an ILVM-13CH3 DnaK/ADP-U-2H TRF1 sample, making use of available assignments for many of the methyl groups of DnaK/ADP (Zhuravleva et al., 2012), as arising from four separate conformers of Ile 401 and Ile 438.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E, and assignments from NOESY experiments.

claim: The interconversion between multiple bound states is slow with a substrate off-rate koff less than 0.3 s−1.
source: In order to estimate the lifetimes of bound states we recorded a magnetization exchange experiment (Farrow et al., 1994) where the appearance of exchange-relayed crosspeaks between HMQC correlations provides evidence of exchange. No such peaks were observed in experiments acquired with a mixing time of 300 ms, establishing that the interconversion between multiple bound states is slow. Simulations that we have performed are consistent with a substrate off-rate, koff, less than 0.3 s−1.
evidence: This is based on magnetization exchange experiments and simulations performed by the authors.

claim: The absence of exchange between bound conformers is consistent with previously measured slow rates of substrate release from DnaK/ADP (~0.001 s−1, 25°C).
source: The absence of exchange between bound conformers is consistent with previously measured slow rates of substrate release from DnaK/ADP (~0.001 s−1, 25°C) (Pierpaoli et al., 1998; Mayer et al., 2000), and in turn also establishes that if DnaK slides between different binding sites on a substrate polypeptide chain (see below) the rate must be on the order of 0.3 s−1 or slower as well.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous kinetic measurements.

claim: A peptide of 16 residues (hTRF123-38) that includes the strongest predicted DnaK binding site shows multiple bound conformations.
source: In order to address this possibility, we synthesized a small peptide of 16 residues, hTRF123-38, that includes the strongest predicted DnaK binding site but lacks the surrounding region and acquired 1H-13C HMQC spectra of IM-13CH3 DnaK/ADP in the free and peptide-bound states (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, left). Notably, extra peaks for DnaK corresponding to Ile 401a,b and Ile 438a,b were observed so that the presence of the entire substrate polypeptide chain is not a pre-requisite for observing multiple bound conformations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Multiple DnaK-bound states of hTRF1 are present even when the lid is not interacting (or interacting less) with substrate in the ATP-bound state.
source: HMQC spectra of hTRF1 bound to DnaK/ATP were recorded using an ATP hydrolysis-deficient variant of the chaperone in which Thr at position 199 was mutated to Ala. The Ile region of the 1H-13C HMQC spectrum of hTRF1 bound to DnaK/ATP shows three separate resonances in addition to the peak from folded (unbound) hTRF1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, with the Leu/Val region showing additional resonances as well. This is similar to what was observed for the DnaK/ADP bound state where the lid is in the closed or down orientation, highlighting that multiple DnaK-bound states of hTRF1 are present even when the lid is not interacting (or interacting less) with substrate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: One substrate sidechain at position 0 extends deep into the hydrophobic pocket of DnaK and is in close proximity (~4 Å) to the δ1-methyl groups of Ile 401 and Ile 438 of the chaperone.
source: High-resolution structures of DnaK-substrate complexes (Zhu et al., 1996; Zahn et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2003) establish that the client protein is partly stabilized by hydrophobic interactions between its sidechains and those of the chaperone that line the binding cavity (Figure 3A). One substrate sidechain, designated to be at position 0 with respect to the DnaK binding cleft, extends deep into the hydrophobic pocket of DnaK and is in close proximity (~4 Å) to the δ1-methyl groups of Ile 401 and Ile 438 of the chaperone (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At least four methyl-containing residues of hTRF1 can occupy the central position of the DnaK binding cleft.
source: In total four separate hTRF1 residues show sets of crosspeaks to Ile 401 and Ile 438 that report on conformational states 'a'-'d' of DnaK (Figure 3B). Thus, at least four methyl-containing residues of hTRF1 can occupy the central position of the DnaK binding cleft (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by NOESY data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Peak 'a' arises from a sub-ensemble of DnaK-bound hTRF1 molecules where Leu 31 is at the 0 position.
source: When Leu 31 was mutated to Ile the peak corresponding to hTRF1 conformation 'a' disappeared from the spectrum (Figure 4), thus establishing that peak 'a' arises from a sub-ensemble of DnaK-bound hTRF1 molecules where Leu 31 is at the 0 position.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peak 'b' arises from Leu 30 at the 0 position.
source: In a similar manner peak 'b' arises from L30 as Lo.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments described in the text.

claim: States 'c' and 'd' correspond to hTRF1 Val residues in the DnaK binding pocket.
source: 1H-13C HMQC spectra of V-13CH3 hTRF1 in complex with U-2H DnaK/ADP establish that states 'c' and 'd' correspond to hTRF1 Val residues in the DnaK binding pocket (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by selective labeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: State 'c' arises from Val 41 at position 0.
source: Since there are only two Val in hTRF1 (Val 18 and Val 41), each was mutated independently to Ile. The resulting spectra of V18I and V41I hTRF1 in complex with DnaK/ADP (Figure 4) lead directly to the assignment of states 'c' and 'd' as arising from Val 41 and Val 18 at position 0, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: State 'd' arises from Val 18 at position 0.
source: Since there are only two Val in hTRF1 (Val 18 and Val 41), each was mutated independently to Ile. The resulting spectra of V18I and V41I hTRF1 in complex with DnaK/ADP (Figure 4) lead directly to the assignment of states 'c' and 'd' as arising from Val 41 and Val 18 at position 0, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: This is the first study where a Val residue has been shown to occupy the 0 position in a DnaK-substrate complex.
source: To the best of our knowledge this is the first study where a Val residue has been shown to occupy the 0 position in a DnaK-substrate complex, although Ile, Leu, Met, Pro and cyclohexylalanine are known to be able to bind in the central pocket (Clerico et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, supported by comparison to known binding residues cited in the literature.

claim: The maxima for states 'a', 'b' and 'd' occur at [DnaK]T/[TRF1]T ratios of 1, indicating that the stoichiometries in these cases are 1 DnaK to 1 hTRF1.
source: The maxima for states 'a', 'b' and 'd', corresponding to complexes with Leu 31, Leu 30 and Val 18 occupying position 0, all occur at [DnaK]T/[TRF1]T ratios of 1, indicating that the stoichiometries in these cases are 1 DnaK to 1 hTRF1 (Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by titration data shown in Figure 5A, B, D.

claim: The maximum for the 'c' state is at a [DnaK]T/[TRF1]T ratio of 2, indicating that this sub-ensemble has two DnaK molecules bound to each hTRF1 chain.
source: Interestingly, however, the maximum for the 'c' state, with Val 41 at 0, is at a ratio of 2, indicating that this sub-ensemble has two DnaK molecules bound to each hTRF1 chain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by titration data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Multiple DnaK molecules have been proposed or modeled to bind large substrate polypeptides such as luciferase and rhodanese.
source: Multiple DnaK molecules have been proposed or modeled to bind large substrate polypeptides such as luciferase (Szabo et al., 1994) and rhodanese (Han and Christen, 2003; Kellner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The data provides evidence for the existence of higher binding stoichiometries than 1:1 at equilibrium in solution even for a small 53 amino acid substrate.
source: Our data provides evidence for the existence of higher binding stoichiometries than 1:1 at equilibrium in solution even for a small 53 amino acid substrate, suggesting that multiple occupancy of closely spaced binding sites on typical substrate molecules (Rüdiger et al., 1997) is indeed possible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the titration data showing 2:1 stoichiometry.

claim: The ratio of Ile 401 resonance intensities for a:b:d at a [DnaK]T/[hTRF1]T value of 1 are 1:0.4:0.05, corresponding to relative Kd values of 1:2.6:20.1 and free energy differences of 0:0.6:1.8 kcal/mol at 35°C.
source: The ratio of Ile 401 resonance intensities for a:b:d at a [DnaK]T/[hTRF1]T value of 1 are 1:0.4:0.05, corresponding to relative Kd values and free energy differences between the states of 1:2.6:20.1 and 0:0.6:1.8 kcal/mol, respectively, at 35°C.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of peak intensities from titration data.

claim: The rotamer distributions for Ile 401 and Ile 438 vary substantially in the different bound conformations.
source: The rotamer distributions for the two Ile residues vary substantially in the different bound conformations, ranging from 42% gauche- for Ile 401 and 100% gauche- for Ile 438 in state 'd', to 99% gauche- for Ile 401 and 46% gauche- for Ile 438 in state 'b'.
evidence: This is based on analysis of 13C chemical shifts shown in Table 1.

claim: Despite being highly conserved in evolution the DnaK binding site residues retain considerable flexibility, allowing the binding pocket to accommodate different substrate sidechains.
source: Thus, despite being highly conserved in evolution the DnaK binding site residues retain considerable flexibility, allowing the binding pocket to accommodate different substrate sidechains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rotamer distribution analysis.

claim: It is not merely the identity of the amino acid residing at position 0 that governs the topology of the binding cleft.
source: Notably, the fractional population of the trans conformer of Ile 438 increases by almost 2-fold, from 28% to 54% between states 'a' and 'b', both of which have a Leu residue at position 0, indicating that it is not merely the identity of the amino acid residing at 0 that governs the topology of the binding cleft.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing rotamer distributions in states 'a' and 'b'.

claim: The β-sandwich domain in the DnaK SBD shows a high degree of conservation within the Hsp70 family of chaperones.
source: The β-sandwich domain in the DnaK SBD shows a high degree of conservation within the Hsp70 family of chaperones (Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The multiplicity of DnaK-substrate conformations should be a common characteristic of Hsp70-client complexes in general.
source: The conserved topology of the substrate binding site suggests that the multiplicity of DnaK-substrate conformations observed presently should be a common characteristic of Hsp70-client complexes in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the binding site.

claim: At least four peaks for Ile 29 are observed in the presence of Hsc70, demonstrating the existence of conformational heterogeneity in the Hsc70-hTRF1 complex.
source: In order to verify this we recorded HMQC spectra of a sample of ILVM-13CH3 hTRF1 containing a two-fold excess of human U-2H Hsc70/ADP (Figure 6). The Ile region of this spectrum clearly shows at least four peaks for Ile 29 in the presence of Hsc70, demonstrating the existence of conformational heterogeneity in the Hsc70-hTRF1 complex as well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three-helix bundle proteins represent ~10% of all in vivo substrates interacting with E.coli DnaK.
source: Three-helix bundle proteins have previously been shown to represent ~10% of all in vivo substrates interacting with E.coli DnaK (Calloni et al., 2012); in addition, conformational heterogeneity has also been detected in the binding of a β-sheet protein with DnaK (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The promiscuity of Hsp70 and the heterogeneous nature of Hsp70-client complexes are general features.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the promiscuity of Hsp70 and the heterogeneous nature of Hsp70-client complexes are general features, beyond what has been characterized in detail in the present study of the DnaK-hTRF1 complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and comparison to other studies.

claim: The residues that are part of the DnaK binding pocket are inherently malleable so that DnaK can recognize and bind to at least four different sites on hTRF1.
source: We find that the residues that are part of the DnaK binding pocket are inherently malleable so that DnaK can recognize and bind to at least four different sites on the small 6 kDa, 53 residue hTRF1 substrate that have been characterized in the present work.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing multiple binding sites and rotamer flexibility.

claim: DnaK will likely bind to multiple client sites on typical client proteins that are much larger than 53 residues.
source: Since typical client proteins of DnaK are much larger than 53 residues, it is very likely that DnaK will bind to multiple client sites, generally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of multiple binding sites on a small substrate.

claim: Binding of Hsp70 at different positions creates sub-ensembles with distinct conformational preferences and different starting structures for folding upon release.
source: Our results, therefore suggest a model for Hsp70-mediated conformational biasing whereby binding of Hsp70 at different positions of a substrate creates sub-ensembles with distinct conformational preferences and hence different starting structures for folding upon release from Hsp70, thereby broadening the conformational space sampled by the substrate as it folds.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 ensemble is a fuzzy complex, characterized by both static and dynamic disorder.
source: More generally, our study establishes that the DnaK-hTRF1 ensemble is a fuzzy complex, characterized by both static and dynamic disorder.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations and conformational dynamics.

claim: The heterogeneity resulting from Hsp70 binding enables the client protein to explore a number of starting conformations as a means for navigating kinetic traps in the conformational free energy landscape.
source: The heterogeneity resulting from Hsp70 binding thus enables the client protein to explore a number of starting conformations, that lead to the formation of different amounts and types of local structure, as a means for navigating kinetic traps in the conformational free energy landscape and for promoting efficient folding to the native state.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Such a mechanism of Hsp70 function is expected to be particularly beneficial for proteins with rugged free energy landscapes and local minima that trap misfolded and aggregation-prone conformations.
source: Such a mechanism of Hsp70 function is expected to be particularly beneficial for proteins with rugged free energy landscapes and local minima that trap misfolded and aggregation-prone conformations, where folding yield is increased by recycling kinetically trapped molecules at the expense of a decrease in folding rate resulting from repeated binding to the Hsp70 chaperone (Agashe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications, supported by a citation.

claim: Slower folding in the presence of the Hsp70 chaperone system has been observed for RNase H.
source: Slower folding in the presence of the Hsp70 chaperone system has indeed been observed in the literature for RNase H (Sekhar et al., 2012a), though such a decrease is predicted to be negligible for fast-folding proteins like hTRF1 (56) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The chaperone-substrate interaction studied here adds to the increasing number of examples of conformational heterogeneity observed in concert with molecular recognition.
source: The chaperone-substrate interaction studied here adds to the increasing number of examples of conformational heterogeneity observed in concert with molecular recognition (Boehr et al., 2009; Mittag et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on conformational heterogeneity in molecular recognition.

claim: In the DnaK-hTRF1 complex, the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface.
source: In the present case the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface, where each sub-ensemble has a well-defined structure, with dissociation and subsequent re-association of the substrate occurring on a slow timescale.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations with slow exchange.

claim: Parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure, resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder.
source: We have shown earlier that parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure (Sekhar et al., 2015, 2016), resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder in these regions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 complex is a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder that enhances exploration of the free energy landscape.
source: Such a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder enhances exploration of the free energy landscape, facilitating the efficient folding of the substrate to its native conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and their functional implications.

claim: The model proposed for Hsp70-mediated protein folding is broadly similar to that proposed for GroEL/ES function.
source: The model proposed above for Hsp70-mediated protein folding is broadly similar to that proposed for GroEL/ES function, wherein GroEL/ES maintains kinetically trapped conformers in a globally unfolded state and subsequently releases them for folding (Weissman et al., 1994; Todd et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison to another chaperone system, supported by citations.

claim: In the case of Hsp70, the starting conformation for substrate folding can potentially be different in every binding cycle.
source: However, in the case of Hsp70 the starting conformation for substrate folding can potentially be different in every binding cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of multiple binding sites.

claim: Hsp70-mediated folding does not rely passively on stochastic refolding from the same conformation, but instead actively alters starting structures as a strategy to sample different folding pathways.
source: Therefore, Hsp70-mediated folding does not rely passively on stochastic refolding from the same conformation, but instead actively alters starting structures as a strategy to sample a different folding pathway and hence different regions of conformational space during each iteration.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The presence of multiple chaperone interaction sites on the substrate is a feature shared between Hsp70, SecB and trigger factor.
source: The presence of multiple chaperone interaction sites on the substrate is a feature shared between Hsp70, SecB (Lilly et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2016) and trigger factor (Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other chaperones.

claim: SecB and trigger factor utilize several surface-exposed hydrophobic pockets for capturing substrate molecules, resulting in a complex where the substrate wraps around the chaperone and buries 4000–8000 Å2 of surface area at the interface.
source: However, SecB and trigger factor utilize several surface-exposed hydrophobic pockets for capturing substrate molecules, resulting in a complex where the substrate wraps around the chaperone and buries 4000–8000 Å2 of surface area at the interface (Lilly et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2016; Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of SecB and trigger factor.

claim: Hsp70 interacts with substrates using predominantly one binding site that contacts the substrate minimally at 4–5 residues, allowing the rest of the chain to explore conformational space.
source: In contrast, Hsp70 interacts with substrates using predominantly one binding site (though interactions with the α-helical lid have been observed previously [Smock et al., 2011]) that contacts the substrate minimally at 4–5 residues, allowing the rest of the chain to explore conformational space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural knowledge and the experimental observations, with a citation.

claim: The mechanism of Hsp70 action is different from those of SecB and trigger factor and appears to be tailored towards its function in assisting protein folding.
source: The mechanism of Hsp70 action is thus different from those of SecB and trigger factor and appears to be tailored towards its function in assisting protein folding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the mechanisms of different chaperones.

claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 interaction is a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder.
source: In the present case the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface, where each sub-ensemble has a well-defined structure, with dissociation and subsequent re-association of the substrate occurring on a slow timescale. We have shown earlier that parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure (Sekhar et al., 2015, 2016), resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder in these regions. Such a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder enhances exploration of the free energy landscape, facilitating the efficient folding of the substrate to its native conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations and conformational dynamics.

claim: Large proteins like luciferase are expected to have several kinetic traps in their folding free energy landscape.
source: Large proteins like luciferase are expected to have several kinetic traps in their folding free energy landscape; in the first binding cycle it is conceivable that only a few sub-ensembles of Hsp70-bound luciferase lead to starting conformations for the client upon release that bypass these kinetic traps and result in efficient folding.
evidence: This is a speculation about the folding behavior of large proteins based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The net probability of folding and hence the folding efficiency increases with the number of iterations that a substrate undergoes through the chaperone cycle.
source: Since only a fraction of folding-competent conformations are generated during any particular iteration of the Hsp70 chaperone cycle, it follows that the net probability of folding and hence the folding efficiency increases with the number of iterations that a substrate undergoes through the chaperone cycle.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Substrate proteins typically undergo multiple rounds of binding and release before folding to the native state.
source: Our data provides a rationale for why substrate proteins typically undergo multiple rounds of binding and release before folding to the native state (Mayer, 2013; Szabo et al., 1994; Clerico et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and explained by the proposed mechanism.

claim: DnaK may be able to bind to the SH3 domain in different ways.
source: Our work also sheds light into the cause of the conformational heterogeneity that was previously reported for a complex between the N-terminal SH3 domain from Drk and DnaK based on the observation of multiple peaks for specific residues in a 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the complex (Lee et al., 2015). While the origin of the peaks was unclear in that study it now appears that DnaK may be able to bind to the SH3 domain in different ways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and a previous study cited.

claim: Multiple modes of binding, including the existence of forward and reverse modes and registry shifts, have been seen in crystal structures of short peptides with DnaK.
source: Multiple modes of binding, including the existence of forward and reverse modes and registry shifts, have also been seen in crystal structures of short peptides with DnaK (Zahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to crystal structures.

claim: Multiple binding modes can exist at equilibrium in solution.
source: Here we establish that such multiple binding modes can exist at equilibrium in solution and we elucidate the molecular determinants for the formation of a heterogeneous chaperone-substrate ensemble.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in solution.
